strengths: Originality: The manuscript presents a distinctive and intuitive architecture in which stripped pretrained transformers communicate through trainable dense-vector edge modules. The construction is end-to-end differentiable and could be useful as a form of pretrained-model composition. Manuscript reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/918681c92c414e24ba6c8b564bdc47d6/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

Significance: Reusing pretrained weights to build larger systems is an important practical problem, and the reported improvements over the Qwen2.5-0.5B vertex model across reasoning, knowledge, and coding benchmarks are promising.

Soundness: The paper evaluates several backbones and applications rather than relying on one benchmark. It also reports unfavorable results honestly: prompting outperforms LMNet for the Qwen models on GSM8K, and the E2E gains vary across metrics.

Presentation: The central architecture, parameter sharing, edge construction, and training stages are understandable, and the tables expose parameter counts, training-token estimates, and several resource figures.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of comparable performance at less than 0.1% of the training cost is not supported by a fair accounting. LMNet inherits a Qwen model trained on 18T tokens, but Table 1 counts only LMNet's additional 0.01T tokens while comparing that number with competitors' entire pretraining. The stated 60 A100 GPU-days, 0.01T tokens, and 1e5 PFLOPs are also not reconciled or derived. Moreover, LMNet is explicitly trained on MMLU, MATH, and GSM8K training data while the comparison models are described as pretraining-only, confounding architectural gains with benchmark-targeted adaptation.

There is no decisive architecture ablation. Comparisons against compute- and parameter-matched stacked transformer layers, repeated applications of the shared backbone, residual adapters, or simpler weight-tied deep networks are missing. Consequently, the experiments do not establish that dense inter-model communication or the proposed topology causes the gains rather than extra depth, added parameters, repeated backbone computation, or supervised training.

The efficiency argument ignores inference and total computation. LMNet-1B invokes 14 full 0.5B transformer vertices and roughly 40 edge blocks per example. Parallelizing same-layer vertices can reduce wall-clock latency only by consuming parallel hardware; it does not reduce total FLOPs. Memory, communication, throughput, latency, and energy are not measured, so the claims of efficiency and environmental friendliness are premature.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The precise data mixture and number of examples from each dataset are omitted; training hyperparameters, schedules, sequence lengths, optimizer settings, sampling and decoding settings, prompts, evaluation implementation, hardware utilization, and random seeds are not provided. Results have no repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests, and the code is only promised for future release.

The adaptation evidence is mixed and sometimes overstated. On E2E, LMNet-1/2/1 trains 36.75M parameters versus LoRA's 0.35M, improves only some metrics, and is worse on MET and CIDEr. On GSM8K, prompting substantially outperforms LMNet for both Qwen backbones. These results do not substantiate a general advantage for limited-data or parameter-efficient adaptation.

The mechanistic analysis does not validate the collective-intelligence interpretation. Different attention maps or projection matrices are expected from independently initialized edge modules and do not prove that every edge is useful or that the topology avoids collapse. Edge-removal, pruning, similarity, causal-intervention, and topology ablations are needed. The displayed GSM8K trace also confuses remaining eggs with muffins despite reaching the correct number.

The theoretical content is weak. Proposition 1 is essentially the chain rule for differentiable modules, while its displayed derivative omits the sums over multiple computational paths. The analogy to universal approximation and claims about emergent behavior, richer information transfer, and capabilities beyond human heuristics are asserted without theory or controlled evidence.

Presentation and responsible-research treatment need substantial improvement. Frequent grammatical errors, duplicated reasoning in Section 5.2.1, ambiguous notation, and tiny appendix visualizations impede interpretation. There is no dedicated limitations or ethics discussion covering dataset licenses, contamination, privacy, harmful outputs, misuse, or the substantial compute footprint; the unmeasured eco-friendly claim is especially inappropriate.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper presents a clear and potentially useful architectural idea—connecting pretrained transformer bodies through trainable hidden-state sequence-to-sequence modules, enabling end-to-end differentiable communication without intermediate token decoding.

The evaluation is broad in surface area: LMNet-1B is tested on 11 general, mathematical, scientific, and coding benchmarks, while customization experiments cover MMLU, GSM8K, and E2E with several backbone models.
Several reported gains are substantial, including improvements over Qwen2.5-0.5B across every Table 1 benchmark and consistent MMLU improvements over prompting and fine-tuning in Table 2.

The paper reports negative results where prompting outperforms LMNet on Qwen-based GSM8K experiments, rather than hiding them. The central construction is also reasonably understandable from the schematic, equations, and tables.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central efficiency comparison is not controlled. LMNet inherits Qwen2.5-0.5B, already trained on 18T tokens, but the claimed “less than 0.1% training cost” counts only LMNet's additional 0.01T-token stage and compares it with the entire pretraining cost of other models. Moreover, LMNet receives MMLU auxiliary data, MATH and GSM8K training splits, and instruction datasets, while the comparison models are described as pretrained-only. This does not establish that the architecture is more efficient than continued training or expanding the same pretrained model under an equal data and compute budget.

The parameter-count comparison is misleading about inference cost. The 1/4/4/4/1 network invokes a full 0.5B transformer at 14 vertices despite parameter sharing. Parallelizing vertices may reduce wall-clock depth given extra hardware, but it does not remove their FLOPs or memory traffic. No latency, throughput, active-compute, memory, or energy measurements support the claims of efficient or eco-friendly scaling.

Crucial controls are absent: compute- and data-matched continued pretraining of Qwen, adding an equivalent number of ordinary transformer layers or adapters, recurrently applying the backbone without learned communication edges, discrete-token communication, and ablations over depth, width, aggregation, edge modules, sharing, and freezing. Consequently, the results do not isolate dense communication or “collective intelligence” as the source of improvement.

The purported mechanistic evidence is insufficient. Different edge weights and attention heatmaps do not prove that every edge is functionally used, that the topology has not collapsed, or that distinct useful messages are communicated. The single GSM8K anecdote is not a systematic intervention or causal analysis and even refers to remaining eggs as muffins.

Reproducibility is poor. Code is only promised for future release, and the paper omits the exact dataset mixture/subset, preprocessing, optimizer, learning rates, batch and sequence sizes, training-phase durations, checkpoint selection, seeds, evaluation harness, decoding settings, and complete prompts. Ambiguous descriptions such as “4/8-shot” and “0/4-shot,” together with no uncertainty estimates or repeated runs, make the reported numbers difficult to verify.

The theoretical support is weak. Proposition 1 is essentially the chain rule for a differentiable computation graph, while the suggested analogy to MLP universal approximation is neither formalized nor proved. Claims that dense vectors carry richer information, reduce communication loss, and enable emergent capabilities are asserted but never directly measured.

Presentation is below conference standard: the manuscript contains frequent grammatical errors, duplicated reasoning in Section 5.2.1, imprecise terminology, and underspecified experimental descriptions. The related-work discussion also does not adequately distinguish LMNet from model stitching, intermediate-representation transfer, ordinary depth expansion, recurrent/shared-weight transformers, soft prompting, and broader latent-reasoning work.

Limitations and ethics are treated inadequately. The future-work section does not candidly analyze the method's high inference compute, dependence on a heavily pretrained backbone, benchmark contamination risk, or scaling constraints. There is also no meaningful discussion of dataset licensing/privacy, inherited model biases and safety behavior, or evidence supporting the environmental claim. Overall, the idea is discernible and promising, but these evidential and reproducibility deficiencies prevent acceptance.

strengths: The core proposal—connecting pretrained transformer modules through learned dense, differentiable sequence-to-sequence edges—is intuitive, potentially useful, and sufficiently distinct to motivate further study. The architecture and intended applications are explained clearly with helpful diagrams. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/ce7f14fa1ac24964a2f24a04d8b06392/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
The empirical scope is broad: LMNet-1B is evaluated on eleven language, reasoning, mathematics, and coding benchmarks, while adaptation experiments cover MMLU, GSM8K, and E2E with several backbones.

Reported improvements over the Qwen2.5-0.5B vertex model are large and consistent in Table 1, including MMLU 44.3→53.9, BBH 20.3→47.3, MATH 19.5→38.8, and HumanEval 30.5→39.0. If confirmed under controlled comparisons, these results would be significant.

The paper studies multiple LMNet topologies and combinations with Prefix Tuning, full fine-tuning, and LoRA. It also honestly reports that LMNet underperforms prompting for the Qwen backbones on GSM8K rather than hiding this negative result.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the principal architecture, parameter sharing scheme, and distinction between vertex and edge parameters are understandable.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central evaluation does not isolate the benefit of dense communication. LMNet-1B is post-trained on Alpaca and on training data from MMLU, MATH, and GSM8K, whereas Table 1 compares it primarily against pretrained-only models that did not receive the same post-training. There is no compute- and data-matched continued-training baseline for Qwen2.5-0.5B, parameter-matched adapter baseline, added-transformer-layer baseline, or weight-tied recurrent-transformer baseline. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed to the proposed topology rather than extra parameters, depth, task-targeted data, or ordinary post-training.

The headline claim of achieving comparable performance with less than 0.1% of the training cost is misleading. LMNet inherits a Qwen model trained on 18T tokens, but this prerequisite cost is excluded while LMNet's 0.01T additional tokens are compared with training competing models from scratch. Parameter count also understates operational cost: the shared 0.5B vertex is executed at many vertices, so LMNet-1B's inference and training FLOPs, latency, memory, and energy are not comparable to those of a conventional 1B model. These quantities are not measured, undermining the efficiency and “eco-friendly” claims.

The evidence for collective intelligence and learned communication roles is inadequate. Most vertices share exactly the same transformer weights, making the construction closer to a deep weight-tied transformer with learned intervening blocks than a collaboration among pretrained models. Different attention maps do not demonstrate that edges convey functionally distinct information, and visually different parameter matrices do not establish that the fully connected topology is necessary or has not collapsed. Edge-removal, shuffling, pruning, topology, aggregation, and weight-sharing ablations are needed.

The limited-data and PEFT comparisons are not well controlled. Training recipes are unspecified, and LMNet often trains far more parameters: on E2E, LMNet-1/2/1 uses 36.75M trainable parameters versus 0.35M for LoRA and PreLayer. Its results are also mixed rather than uniformly superior—for example, its CIDEr of 2.38 is below LoRA's 2.51 and its MET score is below LoRA's 46.5. No variance estimates, repeated runs, or statistical tests are reported despite several small differences.

Reproducibility is insufficient for an ICML empirical paper. The manuscript only promises that code will be released and omits exact data subsets and mixture proportions, preprocessing, optimizer and learning-rate schedules, batch and sequence sizes, phase lengths, random seeds, prompt templates, decoding settings, evaluation harness/version, checkpoint selection, and per-experiment compute. Statements such as “at most 0.01T tokens” and “less than 60 GPU-days” are too imprecise to reproduce the main result.

Originality is promising but incompletely situated. The paper discusses continuous latent reasoning only briefly and does not adequately compare LMNet with model stitching, hidden-state adapters, soft/continuous prompting, recurrent or universal transformers, and depth expansion with parameter sharing. Proposition 1 is merely the standard chain rule for a differentiable network, and the claimed analogy to universal approximation is asserted without a result or proof.

Presentation is readable at the architectural level but contains frequent grammatical errors, duplicated text in the GSM8K discussion, and overstated language about “general intelligence.” Important experimental details are displaced by speculative claims. The qualitative GSM8K example itself confuses remaining eggs with muffins, while Figures 3–4 are not quantitatively analyzed and Figure 4 is difficult to interpret.

Limitations and ethics are not treated adequately. The future-work paragraph mentions scale and architectural extensions but not the unfair cost accounting, much greater inference computation, possible benchmark contamination, evaluation uncertainty, inherited risks of the backbone and training corpora, or downstream misuse. There is no dedicated ethics discussion, and the environmental-benefit claim is unsupported by lifecycle or energy measurements. Overall, the idea has real potential, but the missing controls and reproducibility information leave the paper's central performance and efficiency conclusions unsupported.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper presents an appealing modular view of language models as reusable nodes connected by trainable dense communication edges. Bypassing intermediate tokenization could be useful when model internals are accessible.
Soundness: The proposed architecture is differentiable and technically plausible, and parameter sharing offers a practical way to limit parameter growth.
Empirical scope: Evaluation spans general knowledge, mathematics, coding, and data-to-text generation, multiple backbone families and sizes, and both general training and task adaptation.
Results: The reported gains are often substantial and consistent across backbones, particularly on BBH, MATH, GSM8K, and MMLU.

Presentation/limitations: The main architecture is explained clearly, and the authors candidly acknowledge compute, access, interpretability, and the important mismatch between the motivating agent-communication picture and the implemented token-aligned computation.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central attribution to learned communication is not established. LMNet adds many parameters, repeated backbone evaluations, additional training, and up to 0.02T tokens, yet there is no compute-, parameter-, and data-matched deep/recurrent Transformer or adapter baseline that isolates the communication mechanism.

Soundness: Section 6.3 concedes that the implemented system does not perform sentence-level inter-model message passing and that its gains should be attributed to additional test-time computation with newly learned functions. The method therefore resembles a deeper weight-tied Transformer with inter-block adapters more than the multi-model communication system emphasized throughout the paper.

Evaluation fairness: Table 1 compares a heavily trained LMNet against prompting, test-time sampling, and a vaguely described 'very moderate' SFT. The claimed matching of 14 backbone invocations to 16 samples/iterations is not supported by measured FLOPs, generated-token counts, memory, throughput, or latency, and it does not account clearly for the sizable edge modules.

Evidence for topology claims is weak. Table 6 shows no consistent benefit from greater width or depth, with several 1/1 results matching or exceeding wider networks. Visual differences among independently initialized edge weights do not show that every edge is useful or that the fully connected topology is exploited; edge-removal, routing, and matched sparse/chain ablations are needed.

The communication analysis rests largely on one easy GSM8K example. The procedure for interpreting intermediate states is indirect, and the example does not demonstrate distinct node roles, causal dependence on messages, or systematic emergence of collaboration.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the manuscript leaves the code link blank and omits exact training subsets and mixtures, hyperparameters, schedules, prompts, decoding settings, benchmark implementation details, random seeds, and uncertainty estimates. 'Less than' 0.02T tokens, 100 GPU-days, and 2e5 PFLOPs is insufficient to reproduce the central experiment.

Dataset controls are underspecified. The general model is trained on benchmark training splits and broad public corpora, while OpenR1-Math is used for both added training data and evaluation on an 'unseen subset'; no precise split construction, deduplication, or contamination audit is supplied. The assertion of no test leakage is therefore not verifiable.

Originality is overstated because comparisons and discussion do not adequately distinguish LMNet from deepening or recurrently applying a pretrained Transformer, continuous latent reasoning, and adapter-style inter-layer transformations. The broad 'language model network' formulation itself is mostly a reframing.

Presentation: Several strong conclusions exceed the evidence, including universal-approximation analogies, claims of emergent collective intelligence, and statements that improvements cannot come from training data. The writing also contains frequent grammatical problems and ambiguous implementation descriptions.

Ethics/limitations: The honest limitations discussion is valuable, but the impact statement is boilerplate despite substantial compute usage and opaque latent communication. Energy cost, data licensing/provenance, and risks introduced by reduced interpretability are not meaningfully assessed.

strengths: The paper presents a concrete, end-to-end differentiable architecture that composes pretrained transformer blocks through trainable dense communication modules. Parameter sharing makes the construction more practical than independently replicating every vertex model.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad: experiments cover several backbones and tasks, including MMLU, GSM8K, E2E generation, coding, and larger 3B/7B models. The reported gains are often consistent across backbones.

The manuscript is candid about important limitations. In particular, Section 6.3 acknowledges that the implemented system does not realize the motivating sentence-level inter-model communication and that its gains should instead be attributed to additional learned test-time computation. The discussion also appropriately notes latency, model-access, and interpretability limitations.
The general idea of reusing pretrained models as differentiable modules is potentially useful, especially for supervised adaptation when internal model access is available.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not supported by the experiments. LMNet simultaneously adds substantial sequential computation, depth, trainable edge parameters, and a particular topology. There is no compute- and parameter-matched deep/shared-transformer control, no control using untrained or ordinary adapter layers, and no residual/chain architecture control. Consequently, the results do not establish that dense 'communication' or the network interpretation is responsible for the gains.

The comparisons in Table 1 are not compute-equivalent in a meaningful sense. LMNet applies the 0.5B transformer 14 times per generated position, plus edge modules, while Self-Consistency and Self-Refine use autoregressive trials with materially different execution patterns. Comparing LMNet-1B to monolithic models by stored parameter count in Table 7 is also misleading because LMNet's inference FLOPs resemble repeated use of a much larger model. Latency, FLOPs, memory, generated-token budgets, and wall-clock costs are not reported.

The general-capability experiment trains on the training splits of several reported benchmarks, including MMLU, MATH, and GSM8K. This measures supervised adaptation to those benchmark families rather than an unambiguous improvement in general intelligence. The assertion that all data are free of test leakage is unsupported, particularly given the incompletely specified C4 subset and the use of OpenR1 data. No contamination analysis or clearly independent held-out task suite is provided.

Baseline quality is insufficient. The SFT baseline is described as using 'very moderate training configurations' and substantially degrades performance, but its optimization is not documented or tuned convincingly. LMNet receives a specialized architecture and training schedule without an equally careful compute-matched fine-tuning baseline. COCONUT/CODI and PEFT comparisons likewise lack details needed to verify equal data, optimization, and compute; several E2E numbers are copied from prior work, and LMNet's small metric differences have no uncertainty or significance analysis.

Reproducibility is poor. The displayed code link is empty, and the paper omits exact dataset subsets and mixtures, preprocessing, optimizer settings, learning rates, batch sizes, schedules, training stages, checkpoint selection, decoding settings, prompt templates, random seeds, and per-run variation. Reporting only 'less than 100 GPU-days' and 'less than 0.02T tokens' is not sufficient to reconstruct the main experiment.

The topology analysis does not justify its conclusions. Showing that edge-weight heatmaps differ from initialization does not demonstrate that every edge is functionally used or that the fully connected topology is exploited. Edge pruning, routing interventions, topology ablations, or activation-based causal analyses are needed. The single GSM8K example also cannot establish emergent division of labor, especially because most later nodes merely reproduce the same answer.

The originality is limited relative to stacking/recurrently applying pretrained transformer blocks with shared weights and learned adapters, as well as prior continuous-latent reasoning. The 'language model network' framing is broader than the actual implementation, which uses copies of one shared transformer in a fixed feed-forward graph. The analogy to MLP universal approximation is asserted without a theorem or empirical support.

Presentation is understandable at a high level but contains imprecise claims, grammatical problems, inconsistent table references, and exaggerated language about collective or general intelligence. Claims such as dense vectors carrying 'richer information,' eliminating information loss, and achieving supervision-efficient coordination require controlled evidence.

The limitations discussion is unusually honest, but it omits several decisive limitations: weak causal controls, benchmark-targeted training, lack of statistical uncertainty, incomplete compute accounting, and missing reproducibility details. The impact statement is generic and does not discuss environmental cost or risks from scaling a computation-heavy inference architecture. No acute ethical violation is apparent, but the treatment is cursory.

strengths: The core construction is interesting and potentially useful: pretrained transformers are reused as vertices, while lightweight sequence-to-sequence edge modules transform dense hidden states and permit end-to-end optimization from final-task supervision.

The empirical study has encouraging breadth. It covers general reasoning, mathematics, coding, MMLU and GSM8K adaptation across several backbone families and sizes, and E2E generation against parameter-efficient fine-tuning baselines. Reported improvements are often substantial, such as 20.3 to 47.3 on BBH and 19.5 to 38.8 on MATH for the 0.5B backbone.

Parameter sharing is a practical design choice that limits storage growth, and the paper explicitly reports the added edge parameters. The experiments varying model size, architecture, and training-data volume provide useful preliminary evidence that the approach is not confined to one configuration.

The manuscript is generally organized around a comprehensible node-edge-topology abstraction. It also honestly acknowledges that the implementation does not realize sentence-level message passing and that dense communication increases latency, requires model-internal access, and reduces interpretability.
No major research-ethics concern is apparent from the evaluated public benchmarks and open-model setting, although the impact statement is generic.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not supported by the controls. LMNet applies the full shared backbone 14 times per output token and adds roughly 0.6B edge parameters, but it is not compared against compute- and parameter-matched alternatives such as repeated backbone application with shared or uniform adapters, extra transformer layers, continued pretraining of a similarly sized model, or learned residual recurrence. Comparing primarily with one-pass SFT does not isolate the benefit of network topology or dense communication.

The manuscript itself concedes in Section 6.3 that the gain should currently be attributed to additional test-time computation and newly assigned functions, rather than sentence-by-sentence communication. Consequently, the broad framing as learned inter-model or multi-agent communication overstates what is demonstrated: with shared vertex parameters, the implementation is closer to a recurrent/depth-expanded transformer with branch-specific adapters.

The test-time-scaling comparison is insufficiently specified and potentially unfair. Self-Refine and Self-Consistency receive 16 trials or iterations, but prompts, sampling settings, aggregation, token budgets, and actual FLOPs or latency are not reported. Counting backbone invocations does not match total computation, and Self-Consistency is omitted on coding rather than replaced with an applicable compute-matched baseline.

The general-capability training setup is not reproducible. The paper says only that a small, unspecified subset of several datasets was used, reports broad upper bounds of 0.02T tokens and 100 A100 GPU-days, and omits the exact mixture, optimizer, learning rates, schedules, batch sizes, sequence lengths, training stages, checkpoint selection, seeds, decoding settings, and most prompts. The displayed code link is empty.

The evidence lacks uncertainty estimates, multiple training runs, or significance tests. Several adaptation gains are small—for example, roughly 1–2 accuracy points for the 3B/7B experiments and tied E2E metrics—so conclusions about consistent superiority cannot be assessed independently of run-to-run variation or evaluation choices.

Baseline tuning is not convincing. The main text describes SFT as using 'very moderate' configurations, and SFT actually degrades the base model on many general benchmarks. This does not establish that LMNet extracts benefits specifically from communication; it may instead indicate an under-tuned baseline. The E2E table also mixes newly obtained LMNet results with literature results without establishing identical preprocessing and evaluation implementations.

The communication analysis does not validate the claimed topology conclusions. Different edge weights after training do not show that every edge is functionally used, and visually similar projection matrices cannot rule out redundant paths. Edge removal, learned gates, path interventions, activation analysis, or topology-matched ablations are needed. The behavioral evidence is only one GSM8K example reconstructed through an unusual de-embedding procedure.

The originality discussion omits important neighboring formulations such as recurrent, looped, depth-recurrent, and weight-tied transformers. The analogy from fully connected MLPs to a universal workflow approximator is asserted without a theorem or supporting experiment, and the architecture ablation finds no clear depth/width pattern.

Presentation is readable at a high level but contains imprecise statements and numerous grammatical issues. Claims that de-embedding necessarily 'loses information,' that comparable performance establishes efficient scaling toward general intelligence, and that public training data have no test leakage require substantially more careful qualification. Overall, the idea is promising, but the missing controls and implementation detail leave the main empirical interpretation and reproducibility below the acceptance threshold.
